parameters.name: jacket_closure
parameters.description: Whether the jacket front is single-breasted or double-breasted, affecting formality and visual width

values.definition: Single row of buttons with a narrow overlap. More versatile, can be worn open or closed. Slimmer silhouette.
Two parallel rows of buttons with wide overlap. Incrementally more stylish than single-breasted. Pointed diagonal lapels dress up any worsted. Should be worn buttoned. Projects broader chest.

parameters.visual_effect: DB adds visual width to torso and projects formality. SB is more neutral and versatile.

parameters.name: jacket_button_configuration
parameters.description: Number and arrangement of front buttons on the jacket, affecting the V-opening and visual proportions

values.definition: Single button, lowest stance. Maximum V-opening exposing furnishings. Most elongating. Typically reserved for formal/dinner jackets.
Most popular modern configuration. Lower button stance than three-button, showing more shirt and tie. Gives trimmer look with defined waistline via darts.
Higher button stance, less V-opening. Classic conservative look. Top button optional (often rolled). Shortens perceived torso length.
Three-button jacket where the top button is hidden under a soft lapel roll. Combines the height of a 3-button with the openness of a 2-button. Neapolitan style.
Most common double-breasted: 6 front buttons, 2 that fasten. Broad lapels mark a high waist, straight tails hug hips. Classic DB configuration.
6 front buttons, only bottom one fastens. Lapels roll down below waist, giving illusion of height. Known as the 'Kent' style after Duke of Kent.
4 front buttons, 2 that fasten. More relaxed, laid-back double-breasted look.

parameters.visual_effect: Higher button stance = shorter perceived torso. Lower stance = more elongating. The V-opening frames the shirt/tie and draws the eye upward to the face.

parameters.name: lapel_style
parameters.description: Shape of the jacket lapel, affecting formality and the framing of the face/chest area

values.definition: Standard lapel with a triangular notch where collar meets lapel. Most common on single-breasted jackets. Neutral formality.

Pointed lapels that angle upward toward the shoulders. Standard on double-breasted jackets. On single-breasted, it virtually neutralizes the DB's edge in formality. Spearheaded the popularity of the V-shaped male chest.
Continuous rounded lapel with no notch or peak. Reserved for dinner jackets and tuxedos. Most formal.

parameters.visual_effect: Peak lapels widen the chest visually and direct the eye outward/upward. Notch is neutral. Shawl creates a smooth, formal line.

parameters.name: lapel_width
parameters.description: Width of the jacket lapel measured at its widest point, which should harmonize with tie width and collar spread

values.definition: Under 3 inches. Slims the chest area. Fashion-forward or casual.
3 to 3.5 inches. Classic proportion. Harmonizes with standard tie width.
Over 3.5 inches. Broadens the chest. More traditional/powerful look.

parameters.visual_effect: Wider lapels add visual breadth to the chest. Should match tie width for visual harmony. Rule: lapel width ≈ tie width ≈ collar spread.

parameters.name: gorge_height
parameters.description: Position of the collar-lapel junction (gorge) on the jacket, affecting perceived shoulder line and modernity

values.definition: Below the collarbone. Vintage/classic look. Elongates the lapel line.
At or near the collarbone/shoulder line. Timeless positioning.
Above the shoulder line. Contemporary Italian style. Creates a more modern, shorter lapel look.

parameters.visual_effect: Higher gorge creates a more contemporary look and can make the wearer appear taller. Lower gorge is more classic.

parameters.name: jacket_shoulder_type
parameters.description: Construction and shape of the jacket shoulder, significantly affecting the silhouette and perceived body shape

values.definition: Built-up shoulder with padding. Creates a defined, broad shoulder line. British tradition. Projects authority and width.
Minimal or no padding, following the body's natural shoulder line. American Ivy League/sack suit tradition. Also Neapolitan 'spalla camicia' (shirt shoulder).
Slightly extended with a raised ridge at the sleevehead (spalla con rollino). Neapolitan tradition. Adds subtle width without bulk.
Shoulder line extends beyond the natural shoulder point. Creates illusion of broader shoulders.
Concave/saddle-shaped shoulder (spalla insellata). Dramatic Neapolitan detail.

parameters.visual_effect: Structured shoulders broaden a narrow frame. Soft shoulders suit already-broad shoulders. Extended/padded shoulders add visual width.

parameters.name: jacket_vent_style
parameters.description: Slit(s) at the back of the jacket affecting movement, silhouette, and formality

values.definition: No slit in back. Clean, trim contour. Dressier. But bunches up when sitting or reaching into pockets. Between the wars, most bespoke lounge suits and dinner jackets were ventless.

Single slit at center back. American predilection, Ivy League look. Least expensive to manufacture. Pulls open like a garage door when hand reaches for pocket, revealing the derriere. Least stylish option per Flusser.

Two slits on either side. Highest union of function and form. Permits pocket access while covering buttocks. Leads the eye up either side, imbuing illusion of greater height. Subtle concert of motion between vents and trousers lends fluidity and grace. British tradition.

parameters.visual_effect: Side vents elongate and add grace to movement. Ventless is sleek but restrictive. Center vent is functional but inelegant.

parameters.name: jacket_pocket_type
parameters.description: Style of the jacket's lower pockets, affecting formality and visual bulk

values.definition: Narrow welted slit pockets with no flap. Most formal. Clean, sleek surface. Used on tuxedos and dressier suits. Double-besom construction is the highest quality.
Pockets with a fabric flap covering the opening. Standard formality. Flaps add a layer of fabric, making the jacket slightly less sleek. Can be tucked in for a cleaner look.
Pockets sewn onto the jacket's surface. Most casual. Add another layer to the surface. Would be a sartorial oxymoron on a dark pinstriped suit. Appropriate for sport jackets and light-colored suits.
Diagonally angled flap pockets. Originally from riding/hacking jackets. Chisels breadth away from the hip while adding a line of height. Sporty, slightly Anglicized character.

parameters.notes: Ticket/cash pocket: small extra pocket above the lower hip pocket. Flapped version diminishes dressiness; besom version heightens it.

parameters.name: jacket_silhouette
parameters.description: The overall cut tradition of the jacket, determined by the combination of shoulder, waist, and drape characteristics

values.definition: Structured shoulders, fuller chest with drape, suppressed waist, close-fitting hip. Side vents. The driving force behind tailored fashion in the 1920s-30s.
Natural/unpadded shoulders, undarted straight-hanging body, minimal waist suppression. Soft rolled lapels, three-button front. Ivy League tradition. Brooks Brothers signature.
Soft/minimal shoulder padding, low gorge, lightweight construction. Can range from Neapolitan (unstructured, shirt-shoulder) to Milanese (clean, precise). Generally lighter and more body-conscious.

parameters.visual_effect: British drape creates a V-shaped athletic silhouette. American sack is relaxed and straight. Italian is body-conscious and light.

parameters.name: jacket_sleeve_buttons
parameters.description: Number of buttons on the jacket sleeve cuff, a subtle marker of sartorial attention

values.definition: Minimal, clean. Acceptable on two-button jackets.
Often used on summer/lighter jackets. Harmonizes with three-button front.
Standard on suit jackets. Conveys superior sartorial breeding per London tradition. Buttons set close together with edges 'kissing.'

parameters.notes: Working/surgeon's cuffs (functional buttonholes) are a bespoke marker. Bottom button should finish no more than 3/4 inch above the sleeve bottom.

parameters.name: jacket_construction
parameters.description: Internal construction method affecting drape, shape retention, and quality

values.definition: Interlining glued to outer fabric. Budget construction. Can bubble over time. Less natural drape.
Canvas interlining in upper chest and lapels only. Good balance of quality and cost. Lapels roll naturally.
Canvas throughout entire front panel. Highest quality. Molds to the wearer's body over time. Best drape and shape retention.

parameters.visual_effect: Full canvas creates the most natural, fluid drape. Fused jackets appear stiffer and less organic.

parameters.name: jacket_formality_tier
parameters.description: Hierarchical formality ranking of tailored upper garments

values.definition: Matched with trousers of same fabric. Highest formality in daily wear. Should not be worn as a standalone piece.

Ranks between suit and sport jacket in dressiness. Metal buttons (brass/gilt/nickel/mother-of-pearl). Chameleon-like versatility — works with flannels, jeans, shorts. DB blazer is slightly more formal than SB.
Most casual of tailored jackets. 'Odd' detailing: bellows pleats, action backs, patch pockets, bold patterns. Not meant to be mistaken for a suit jacket.

parameters.notes: Within each tier: DB > SB, flap pockets > patch, peaked lapels > notched, side vents > center vent, dark trousers > light trousers — each increments formality.

parameters.name: trouser_front
parameters.description: Whether trousers have pleats and their configuration, affecting comfort, drape, and formality

values.definition: No pleats. Clean, slim appearance. Pared-down, uncluttered simplicity. Low rise and form-fitting contour.
One pleat on each side. Moderate fullness.

Two pleats on each side — a deep one near the fly and a shallower one toward the pocket. Classic design. The smaller pleat helps the larger one remain closed. More than two pleats is a fashion gimmick.
Pleat folds face toward the fly/center. Traditional English style.
Pleat folds face toward the pocket/side seam. Most common in ready-to-wear.

parameters.visual_effect: Pleats look dressier and provide comfort. Flat-front is slimmer and more modern. Pleats accommodate hip widening when seated.

parameters.name: trouser_rise
parameters.description: Distance from crotch seam to waistband top, determining where trousers sit on the body

values.definition: Sits at the natural waist (near navel). Classical positioning. Returned in the 1980s with pleats and suspenders. Creates ideal balance between jacket and trousers.
Sits between natural waist and hip bones. Modern standard for most ready-to-wear.
Sits at or below the hip bones. If waistband rests between natural waist and hip, the ideal balance between jacket and trousers is doomed per Flusser.

parameters.visual_effect: High rise elongates the legs visually. Low rise shortens the leg line and can cause jacket-trouser proportion imbalance.

parameters.name: trouser_break
parameters.description: Amount of fabric that folds at the front crease where the trouser meets the shoe

values.definition: Hem just above the shoe with no horizontal fold. Clean, modern, slightly shorter appearance.
Minor horizontal crease/dimple where trouser meets shoe. Most versatile and recommended.
Moderate fold of fabric over the shoe. Traditional business standard.
Significant fabric pooling on the shoe. More casual, can look sloppy if unintentional.

parameters.visual_effect: Less break creates a cleaner, more elongating line. Full break can shorten apparent leg length.

parameters.name: trouser_cuff
parameters.description: Whether trouser hems are turned up (cuffed) or left plain, affecting visual weight at the ankle

values.definition: Trouser hem turned up, typically 1.5-2 inches. Adds visual weight at the bottom. Helps the trouser hang straight. Cuffed bottoms and crease significantly improve the line of a trouser. Not used on formal trousers.
Plain hem with no turn-up. Required for formal wear. Creates a slightly longer, uninterrupted leg line.

parameters.visual_effect: Cuffs add horizontal line at ankle (shortening effect) but also weight that improves drape. Short men should use narrower cuffs or skip them.

parameters.name: trouser_width
parameters.description: Width of the trouser leg, particularly at the knee and hem

values.definition: Tapered, body-conscious cut. Modern/fashion-forward. Narrower through thigh and hem.
Medium width with gentle taper from thigh to hem. Classic proportion.

Generous width allowing natural drape and movement. Full across hip and thigh, tapering to bottom. Classical tailoring tradition. Long, wide trousers supported the columnar, athletic silhouette of the 1920s-30s.

parameters.visual_effect: Fuller trousers add volume and can balance a broader upper body. Slim trousers elongate but expose leg shape.

parameters.name: trouser_waistband
parameters.description: Fastening method at the trouser waist, affecting silhouette and formality

values.definition: Standard loops for a belt, 1.25 to 1.5 inch width. Most common modern construction.
Tab adjusters on either side of the waist. Cleaner waistline without belt bulk. Also known as side tabs.
Buttons inside waistband for braces/suspenders. Allows trousers to hang from shoulders. Cleaner drape.
Matching fabric belt integrated into the waistband. Removed the bother of a separate belt. Popular for resort and casual wear. Fastened with D-ring.
Self-supporting beltless trouser with internal elastic and side tabs. First self-supporting beltless trouser, invented 1932. Comfort-in-action design.
One-piece front and back with narrow belt loops positioned below the trouser's top. Created in the 1930s. Requires narrow belts.

parameters.name: shirt_collar_style
parameters.description: Shape and style of the dress shirt collar, which frames the face and must harmonize with face shape, tie knot, and jacket lapels

values.definition: Standard collar with points angled downward. Most stylisticaly neutral. Points should be 2.75 to 3.375 inches long. Narrow opening between points favors a rounder, oval face rather than narrow one.

Collar points spread apart at a wider angle. Keystone of the English bespoke look since the 1920s. Inherently dressy and elegant. Wider spread counters narrow faces. Several models available to flatter any head shape.
Extreme spread where points angle almost horizontally or backward. Most formal spread variant. Also called Windsor collar.

Collar points fastened to shirt front with buttons. American contribution to dress shirt fashion. Quintessential Ivy League. Can be dressed up or down. Less formal than other collar types. Projects casual elegance.

Collar with small fabric tabs that connect behind the tie knot, pushing the knot up and forward. Raises the tie knot higher on the neck. Functions like a pin collar. Adds extra measure of nattiness but demands precision in execution.

Collar points connected by a decorative pin underneath the tie knot. Raises the knot, creating an elegant arch in the tie. Demands a bit more aplomb. Once worn by half of all American men. Pointed ends work to counterpoint the rounded or oval contour of chin.
Collar with rounded points instead of sharp ones. Vintage style. Originated in Eton College. Less common today.
Small standing collar with folded-down tips (wings). Reserved for formal evening wear with bow ties.

parameters.visual_effect: Collar frames the face like a picture frame. Spread collars widen a narrow face. Point collars narrow a wide face. Collar height must suit neck length — longer necks need higher collars. Small collars make a large head appear larger.

parameters.name: shirt_collar_height
parameters.description: Height of the collar band that sits around the neck, which must relate to the wearer's neck length

values.definition: Short collar band sitting lower on the neck. Casual. Can make neck appear longer.
Medium height collar band. Appropriate for most neck lengths.
Higher collar band sitting higher on the neck. More formal. Italian tradition. Long necklines require higher-sitting collars to maintain proper proportion.

parameters.visual_effect: Collar height should be proportional to neck length. A long neck is best balanced by a higher collar. A short neck needs a lower collar to avoid looking compressed.

parameters.name: shirt_collar_stiffness
parameters.description: The firmness or softness of the collar fabric, affecting its drape and formality

values.definition: Unfused, natural drape. Casual feel. Pairs with natural-shoulder jackets. Button-down collars are inherently soft.
Light interlining for some structure. Most versatile.
Heavily fused or starched for crisp, formal appearance. A full face that sags around chin or cheeks demands a stiffer collar to counteract effects of age and gravity.

parameters.name: shirt_cuff_style
parameters.description: Style of the shirt sleeve cuff, affecting formality and what accessories are worn

values.definition: Standard button cuff. Can have 1-3 buttons. Most common and versatile. Less formal.
Folded-back cuff fastened with cufflinks. More formal. The 'showing linen' — exposing shirt cuff at the wrist — was historically a sign of gentility.
Can be fastened with either buttons or cufflinks. Versatile.

parameters.visual_effect: Shirt cuffs should show 1/2 to 3/4 inch below jacket sleeve. This 'showing linen' at the wrist is one of Flusser's 5 key body intersections.

parameters.name: tie_knot_type
parameters.description: Method used to tie the necktie, producing different knot sizes and shapes that must harmonize with collar spread

values.definition: Small, slightly asymmetrical knot. Most versatile and classic. Works best with point and button-down collars. Uses least tie length.
Medium, symmetrical triangular knot. Works well with spread and semi-spread collars.
Large, symmetrical triangular knot. Designed for wide spread/cutaway collars. Flusser warns against its bulbous mass forcing truncated collar points farther off the chest.
Medium, symmetrical knot tied inside-out. Good alternative to Half-Windsor.

parameters.visual_effect: Knot size must fill the collar opening — outer borders of tie knot should correspond with inner borders of the collar. Too-small knot in wide spread looks lost; too-large knot in narrow collar forces points apart.

parameters.name: tie_width
parameters.description: Width of the necktie blade at its widest point, which should harmonize with lapel width

values.definition: Under 2.5 inches. Fashion-forward, casual. Pairs with narrow lapels.
2.5 to 3 inches. Modern proportion.
3.25 to 3.5 inches. Classic width. Harmonizes with standard lapels.
Over 3.5 inches. Traditional/vintage proportion.

parameters.visual_effect: Tie width should roughly match jacket lapel width for visual harmony. Mismatched widths create visual imbalance.

parameters.name: tie_length
parameters.description: Where the tie blade tip terminates relative to the waistband

values.definition: Tip reaches the trouser waistband or belt buckle center. Ideal length. Both blades should be close in length.
Tip ends above the belt. Too short. Exposes the narrow end behind.
Tip hangs below the belt. Too long. Looks sloppy and shortens the torso visually.

parameters.name: tie_dimple
parameters.description: Whether the tie has a pinched crease/dimple just below the knot

values.definition: Pinched crease below the knot creating a small indentation. Adds dimension, texture, and elegance. Sign of sartorial attention.
Flat, smooth tie below the knot. Simpler, less fussy.

parameters.name: suit_piece_count
parameters.description: Number of matched pieces in the suit ensemble

values.definition: Jacket and matching trousers. Modern standard.

Jacket, matching trousers, and matching waistcoat/vest. The waistcoat adds gravitas, holds tie in place, keeps shirt tidy, lends efficient appearance when in shirtsleeves. Prior to WWII, most suits were three-piece.

parameters.visual_effect: Waistcoat adds a layer of formality, covers the trouser waistband, and provides additional opportunity for visual interest via odd waistcoats.

parameters.name: blazer_button_material
parameters.description: Material of blazer buttons, affecting formality and character

values.definition: Traditional blazer button. Classiest is plain, flat English gilt with shank. Implies gentility and tradition.
Dulled nickel or pewter shade. Good for men with gray hair or predominantly gray-toned trousers.
Off-white buttons. Option for brighter blue tropical wool or linen blazers.
Dark brown horn. First non-metal alternative considered. But its dullish character lacks personality to offset the dark jacket.

parameters.name: odd_trouser_fabric_formality
parameters.description: Hierarchy of odd trouser fabrics from dressy to casual, as paired with blazers or sport jackets

values.definition: The blue blazer of odd trousers. Medium gray worsted accommodates a larger variety of sport coats than any other trouser. First alternate to charcoal gray for blazer pairing.
Silky smooth worsted offering textural change from rough flannel. One of the most lustrous lengths of worsted ever to grace a male thigh.
Slightly lighter shade of gray or tan family. Produces slightly more contrast than gray under average sport coat, registering a slight drop in relative dressiness.
Ribbed fabric. Step down from covert in dressiness. Works in regular weights and variegated ribs. Cotton cords perfect for campus or outdoor activities.
Olive drab cotton. Became campus uniform after WWII. Classic casual trouser.
Blue jeans. Bottom of the dress-down meter. Most casual pairing with blazer or sport jacket.

parameters.notes: Hierarchy for blazer pairing: charcoal gray > medium gray worsted/flannel > tan covert/gabardine > corduroy > chino > jeans.

garment_harmony_principles.name: width_harmony_rule
garment_harmony_principles.description: Tie width, lapel width, and collar spread should be approximately equal for visual balance

garment_harmony_principles.name: collar_face_matching
garment_harmony_principles.description: Collar style should complement face shape: spread collars widen narrow faces, point collars narrow wide faces. Collar height should match neck length. Small collars make large heads appear larger.

garment_harmony_principles.name: knot_collar_fill
garment_harmony_principles.description: The tie knot should fill the collar opening appropriately — outer borders of the knot should correspond with inner borders of the collar points.

garment_harmony_principles.name: formality_consistency
garment_harmony_principles.description: All elements should be at roughly the same formality level. Flap pockets > patch, peaked > notched, side vents > center vent, dark trousers > light, DB > SB — each increments or decrements formality.

garment_harmony_principles.name: showing_linen_principle
garment_harmony_principles.description: The shirt collar should sit above the jacket collar (showing 1/2 inch) and shirt cuffs should show 1/2 to 3/4 inch below jacket sleeves. These are two of Flusser's five critical body intersections.

garment_harmony_principles.name: trouser_jacket_balance
garment_harmony_principles.description: Trouser rise must be high enough that the waistband sits at or near the natural waist for ideal visual balance between jacket and trousers. Low-rise trousers doom this balance.

garment_harmony_principles.name: stripe_elongation_effect
garment_harmony_principles.description: Vertical elements (stripes, side vents, hacking pockets, peak lapels) create illusion of height. Horizontal elements (cuffs, wide lapels, pocket flaps, double-breasted closure) add visual width.
